lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Life Cycle of the Grasshopper, Incomplete Metamorphosis

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Draw the stages of the life cycle of a grasshopper from egg through nymph to adult.
- Identify the behaviour of each stage of the life cycle of a grasshopper.
- Explain why the life cycle of the grasshopper is described as incomplete metamorphosis, as compared to the complete metamorphosis seen in the housefly and mosquito studied in earlier grades.

pages.title: What is Metamorphosis?
pages.body: Metamorphosis is the process by which an insect changes in form and structure as it develops from a young stage into an adult. Complete metamorphosis and incomplete metamorphosis are the two broad patterns insects follow, and comparing them helps explain why the grasshopper, studied in this lesson, develops so differently from insects such as the housefly and the mosquito, studied in earlier grades.

pages.title: The Egg Stage
pages.body: The grasshopper life cycle begins when an adult female lays a cluster of eggs in the soil, usually protected within a tough, frothy case that hardens to shield the eggs from predators and drying out. The eggs remain in the soil, often over an entire dry season, before hatching when conditions become favourable, typically at the start of the rainy season.

pages.title: The Nymph Stage
pages.body: When a grasshopper egg hatches, it produces a nymph, a young grasshopper that already resembles a small, wingless version of the adult, actively feeding on leaves and grasses from the moment it hatches. As the nymph grows, its hard outer skin (exoskeleton) becomes too tight, so the nymph moults, shedding its old exoskeleton and growing a new, larger one underneath. A nymph moults several times as it grows, and with each successive moult, small wing buds on its back become larger and more developed, until, after the final moult, the wings are fully formed.

pages.title: The Adult Stage
pages.body:
Once a nymph completes its final moult and its wings are fully developed and functional, it becomes an adult grasshopper, capable of flying and reproducing. Adult grasshoppers continue feeding actively on plant material, and mature females eventually lay their own eggs, beginning the cycle again.

[[pic:A labelled life cycle diagram of the grasshopper arranged in a circular loop, showing eggs in soil, then a small wingless nymph, then a larger nymph with visible wing buds, then a fully winged adult grasshopper, with curved arrows connecting each stage back to a female adult laying eggs to complete the loop.]]

Notice that, unlike some other insects, the grasshopper nymph already resembles a smaller version of the adult from the moment it hatches, gradually growing larger wings through each successive moult rather than passing through a completely different body form.

pages.title: Behaviour at Each Stage
pages.body: Feeding, growing and reproducing describe the general behaviour pattern that runs through the grasshopper life cycle, though the specific behaviour differs at each stage. The egg stage shows no active behaviour, since the egg simply remains dormant in the soil until conditions favour hatching. The nymph stage is characterised by almost constant feeding on leaves and grasses, rapid growth, and repeated moulting, but nymphs cannot yet fly or reproduce. The adult stage adds flight and reproduction to the ongoing feeding behaviour, with adult grasshoppers able to disperse over wider areas in search of food and mates, and females seeking out suitable soil in which to lay their eggs.

lessons.title: Why the Grasshopper Shows Incomplete Metamorphosis

pages.title: Why the Grasshopper Shows Incomplete Metamorphosis
pages.body:
Incomplete metamorphosis describes a life cycle with only three stages, egg, nymph and adult, in which the nymph already resembles a smaller, wingless version of the adult and gradually develops into the adult form through a series of moults, without ever passing through a resting, non feeding stage. This is exactly the pattern seen in the grasshopper. Complete metamorphosis, by contrast, as seen in the housefly and the mosquito studied in earlier grades, involves four distinct stages, egg, larva, pupa and adult, in which the larva looks nothing like the adult, and the pupa is a resting stage during which the insect's body is almost completely rebuilt before it emerges in its final adult form.

The key difference, then, is that a grasshopper nymph is already active, feeding, and recognisably grasshopper shaped, simply lacking full sized wings and reproductive maturity, whereas a housefly or mosquito larva looks completely different from the adult and must pass through an inactive pupal stage before its body is transformed into the adult form.

pages.title: More About Each Stage of the Life Cycle of the Grasshopper
pages.body:
| **STAGE** | **DESCRIPTION** | **BEHAVIOUR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Egg** | The female pushes her ovipositor, the pointed end of her abdomen, into moist soil and lays a group of eggs in a frothy case called an egg pod. One pod may hold several dozen eggs | The eggs lie in the soil for weeks or months and hatch when the rains come |
| **Nymph, or hopper** | It looks like the adult but is smaller, has no wings and cannot reproduce. It sheds its outer skin, or moults, about five times. Small wing buds appear and grow larger after each moult | It hops but cannot fly. It feeds on leaves and grows quickly |
| **Adult** | It has two pairs of fully formed wings, strong hind legs for jumping and can reproduce | It flies and hops, feeds on leaves, mates, and the female lays eggs |

| **FEATURE** | **INCOMPLETE METAMORPHOSIS** | **COMPLETE METAMORPHOSIS** |
|---|---|---|
| **Number of stages** | Three, which are egg, nymph and adult | Four, which are egg, larva, pupa and adult |
| **Appearance of the young** | The nymph looks like the adult | The larva looks quite different from the adult |
| **Pupa stage** | Absent | Present |
| **Food of young and adult** | Usually the same | Often different |
| **Examples** | Grasshopper, cockroach, termite | Housefly, mosquito, butterfly |

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Other insects that undergo incomplete metamorphosis, similar to the grasshopper, include cockroaches, termites and true bugs, all of which produce nymphs that resemble smaller versions of the adult. Recognising whether an insect undergoes complete or incomplete metamorphosis can be a useful clue when trying to identify or manage a particular insect, since the two patterns often require different control strategies in agriculture and pest management.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Outline the activities of the grasshopper in everyday life, for example feeding on grasses and weeds.
- Carry out a search for information on activities of the grasshopper that are harmful or beneficial to humans.
- Generate activities to promote or reduce the effect of the activities of grasshoppers on humans.

pages.title: Everyday Activities of the Grasshopper
pages.body: Feeding, moving and reproducing describe the main everyday activities of the grasshopper, and each of these activities has consequences, some helpful and some harmful, for the humans who share the environment with them. Grasshoppers feed almost continuously on plant material, particularly grasses, weeds and the leaves of many food crops, using their strong mouthparts to chew through vegetation. They move by walking, jumping with their powerful hind legs, and, once adult, flying to new areas in search of food, often in response to changes in food availability or weather. Adult females lay eggs in the soil, allowing the population to continue into the next season.

questions.e: Adult grasshoppers continue feeding actively on plant material, and mature females eventually lay their own eggs, beginning the cycle again.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Harmful Effects of Grasshopper Activity on Humans

pages.title: Harmful Effects of Grasshopper Activity on Humans
pages.body: Crop destruction, reduced food supply, and economic loss for farmers are the main harmful effects linked to grasshopper activity, particularly when grasshopper populations grow very large. A small number of grasshoppers feeding in a field usually causes only minor damage, but large swarms, sometimes involving related insects such as locusts, can strip entire fields of maize, millet, rice and vegetables within a short time, destroying a farmer's harvest and threatening food security for an entire community. Repeated crop damage can also discourage farmers from investing in certain crops, affecting long term agricultural planning in an affected area.

pages.title: Beneficial Effects of Grasshopper Activity on Humans
pages.body:
Serving as food, supporting other animals, and contributing to nutrient cycling are beneficial effects linked to grasshopper activity that are sometimes overlooked. In many parts of the world, including parts of Africa, grasshoppers are collected and eaten as a nutritious source of protein. Grasshoppers also form an important part of the diet of many birds, reptiles and other predators, supporting broader food webs in an ecosystem. Additionally, grasshopper droppings and the eventual decomposition of dead grasshoppers return nutrients to the soil, contributing in a small way to natural nutrient cycles such as the nitrogen cycle studied earlier in this strand.

[[pic:A split image showing two contrasting scenes, on one side a farm field with visibly damaged, chewed maize leaves and a caption reading Harmful, crop damage, and on the other side a bowl of roasted grasshoppers prepared as food alongside a bird eating a grasshopper, with a caption reading Beneficial, food source.]]

Notice that the same organism can have both harmful and beneficial effects depending on the situation, which is why managing grasshopper populations sensibly, rather than simply trying to eliminate them completely, is usually the more balanced approach.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Managing the Effects of Grasshoppers on Humans

pages.title: Managing the Effects of Grasshoppers on Humans
pages.body: Monitoring populations, using targeted control methods, and encouraging beneficial uses are three general strategies for managing the balance between the harmful and beneficial effects of grasshopper activity. Farmers and agricultural extension officers can monitor grasshopper numbers in a farming area, allowing early warning before a small population grows into a damaging swarm. Where numbers become excessive, targeted methods, such as approved insecticides used carefully and sparingly, or encouraging natural predators such as birds, can help reduce crop damage without harming the wider environment. At the same time, communities that value grasshoppers as a food source can promote sustainable harvesting for consumption, turning a potential pest problem into a nutritional and economic opportunity.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Locusts, which are actually a type of grasshopper capable of forming enormous, highly destructive swarms under certain environmental conditions, have historically caused some of the most severe agricultural crises in parts of Africa and the Middle East. Understanding the basic biology and behaviour of grasshoppers, including their life cycle studied in Lesson 3, helps scientists and farmers predict and respond to locust outbreaks before they cause widespread crop destruction.
